title: SDO watches the Sun every twelve seconds
description: The Solar Dynamics Observatory has been imaging the Sun in multiple wavelengths since 2010, delivering about one point five terabytes of data each day. This short explores flares, magnetic loops and eruptions captured in stunning detail.

shots.narration: Since its 2010 launch, SDO has watched the Sun nonstop, recording this bright flare and erupting loops.
SDO images the full solar disk every twelve seconds, revealing active regions in ultraviolet and extreme ultraviolet wavelengths.
Here, glowing plasma follows magnetic field lines, forming loops larger than many Earths.
A large flare erupts, releasing energy equal to millions of hydrogen bombs.
The eruption launches a coronal mass ejection, a particle cloud that reaches Earth in one to three days.
From this full‑disk view, the Sun’s surface shines at five thousand five hundred degrees Celsius, its corona over a million degrees.
Each flash reaches Earth in eight minutes twenty seconds, delivering light that sustains climate and life.
The Sun’s magnetic poles reverse roughly every eleven years, reshaping loop and eruption patterns.
Through constant vigilance, SDO records the Sun’s breathing, turning fleeting drama into a continuous story.
